newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Volvo sees profits in Indian oil shock.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Volvo sees profits in Indian oil shock.

text.p: While most Indians are dreading the prospect of an impending petroleum price hike, one company is quietly eyeing a big business opportunity in it.

Swedish auto-maker Volvo AB is hoping that an oil shock, due when India cuts state subsidies on diesel, will bring home to Indian customers the low-cost logic of the heavy cargo trucks it plans to roll out a year from now.

"We are giving to India what India needs," Ravi Uppal, managing director of Volvo's Indian subsidiary, told Reuters in an interview at the southern city of Bangalore, where the firm laid the foundation stone for its truck project in April.

Volvo India Private Limited plans to roll out its first truck with a gross weight of 16 tonnes or more by April 1998 from the 3.0-billion rupee ($83.7 million) plant near Bangalore, which would have a capacity to make up to 4,000 trucks a year.
The plant would be Volvo's first full-scale manufacturing facility in Asia, where it currently has assembly shops or plants in Malaysia, Thailand and Pakistan.

"This is a high-profile project within the Volvo group," Uppal said. "The Indian project is going to be key for Southeast Asia....Once we stabilise manufacturing and quality, we would definitely consider supplying to other markets."
With India's annual industrial growth hovering around 10 percent, Volvo officials believe the commercial transport sector will play a key role by oiling the wheels of the economy.

India's medium-range trucks of 10-15 tonnes gross weight can carry a net load of seven to eight tonnes, while Volvo plans to shift net loads of up to 33 tonnes on its multiple-axle vehicles fitted with trailers, which can have a gross weight as high as 49 tonnes.
At the same fuel efficiency of four km (2.5 miles) per litre of diesel, a big truck could carry up to four times the weight of medium-range trucks, Uppal said.
India's oil pool deficit is estimated at around 155 billion rupees ($4.33 billion), and the country's leaders have warned of a fuel price hike that is expected to be announced any day.
"Diesel is becoming dearer. Subsidies are being withdrawn," Uppal said. "People are going to look for cheaper per-tonne, per-kilometre cost."
Volvo plans to make the prime movers of the trucks and separately build its own rear-end trailers, currently being made in India by small companies, Uppal said.
He said Volvo's trailers would be superior in quality, and the company would offer strong after-sales service to better India's informal roadside workshops.
Volvo officials believe a key advantage it holds is the efficient engineering of multiple axles.
Volvo entered India under a six-year-old economic liberalisation programme that has ushered in many international companies, including auto makers.
Uppal said India's current economic growth would fuel a need for 40-foot and 20-foot containers and air-conditioned trucks to carry perishable cargo like seafood, vegetables and flowers.
"Conventional trucks are not going to provide what international customers are looking for," Uppal said.
"You have to do bulk transport at a much lower cost," he said. "We are world leaders. That is where we see a position for us to come in."
India's economy grew at an estimated 6.8 percent in 1996/97 (April-March). Indian officials are now predicting 7.0 percent growth in 1997/98 and aiming for an 8.0 percent growth rate.

Volvo, which has yet to work out the exact size and price of its trucks aimed at the Indian market, sold 63,700 trucks of varying sizes worldwide in 1996, accounting for sales worth $6.6 billion and a market-share of 9.0 percent in heavy trucks.

In India, Volvo has been the first to jump into the heavy truck segment in which it competes elsewhere with Sweden's Scania, France's Renault and Germany's Mercedes Benz AG, part of the Daimler Benz group.
India spells an opportunity for Volvo, but also risks.

"We are the ones to bell the cat," Uppal said, adding the very idea of heavier bulk transportation had to be sold to Indian customers who were so far content with medium-range trucks. "A lot of concept selling has to be done," he said.
To begin with, Volvo is targeting transport companies with big fleets and large steel and cement makers with their own trucks.
"We are right now doing a detailed market research study but I would say we have very good signals from the market," Uppal said.
He added that Volvo's trucks might compete with medium-sized trucks, but lighter trucks and vans were expected to complement the big trucks by offering transport within cities and suburbs.

Volvo is also exploring the possibility of selling big passenger buses, for which it is carrying out a detailed feasibility study, but Volvo officials say India is not ready to yield sufficient demand for its cars, which are targeted at the affluent. ($1=35.8 rupees)
